 KAI’S TAKE: NC State has momentum. Can the Pack bring it to Charlotte against No. 14 Kentucky?
 Published
 6 hours ago on
 November 8, 2026 
 By
 Kai Crutchfield 
 It’s game day, folks! 
 No. 25 NC State. No. 14 Kentucky. A neutral floor in Charlotte. 3PM today on ESPN2. 
 Two comfortable wins are in the books for the Pack. Now we get a different kind of conversation. 
 Can State create the same opportunities against more size? Can the defense stay aggressive without leaving somebody scrambling behind it? And when Kentucky makes that first run, how does the Pack respond? 
 Let’s get into it. 
 Different jerseys. Two very familiar coaches. 
 There isn’t a whole lot of history between these programs. NC State and Kentucky have met just 7 times, with the Pack winning the last 3. 
 But Wes Moore and Kenny Brooks? 
 Oh, they know each other. 
 Kenny Brooks spent 8 years at Virginia Tech, where he and Moore coached against each other 15 times. Those games became a very different proposition as Kenny Brooks built that program. 
 January 2021. No. 2 NC State. Overtime in Blacksburg. Virginia Tech handed us a loss that night. I played in that one, and it still hurts my heart a little. Kenny Brooks finished his Virginia Tech tenure with 4 straight wins against State, including the Hokies’ first win at Reynolds in 2023. 
 But one of my favorite stories from that stretch happened after State beat Tech in the 2022 ACC Tournament. 
 Kenny Brooks asked to speak to State’s team. Moore asked to speak to Tech’s. 
 They swapped locker rooms. 
 Think about that. Two coaches competing for the same conference championship, willing to walk into the other locker room and pour into those players. 
 The respect is there. 
 So is the competitiveness. 
 Now Kenny Brooks brings Clara Strack, Moore brings Khamil Pierre, and we get another chapter in Charlotte. 
 Kentucky has the talent. State needs to test the chemistry. 
 Kentucky lost 8 players from last season and returned 2 starters. 
 That is a lot to replace. 
 Kenny Brooks answered with transfers and a freshman class that includes 3 McDonald’s All-Americans. The names have changed, but the expectations certainly haven’t. Kentucky opened with a 43-point win over Morehead State, then beat Northern Kentucky 79–28. Impressive margins. But neither game required Kentucky to navigate much pressure. 
 Can State make this new group uncomfortable? 
 Make the ball handler change direction. Disrupt the first action.  Force players to communicate through a possession instead of letting them get straight to what they practiced. 
 That’s where State’s returning experience could help.  
 It doesn’t guarantee cleaner execution, but the Pack should understand what it wants to create. 
 The opportunity is to make Kentucky work through newer chemistry. 
 Clara Strack makes you defend more than the block 
 Let’s talk about the 6-foot-5 problem in the middle. 
 Strack averaged 16.9 points and 10.1 rebounds last season, with 16 double-doubles and 91 blocks. 
 But saying “protect the paint” doesn’t cover everything she can do. 
 Strack can catch at the elbow, face up and make that jumper. She can screen and pop instead of rolling straight to the rim. She can move away from the action and take her defender with her; creating more room for the guards to operate.  
 So how does State make her work before she even gets the ball? 
 Start the matchup early. 
 Beat her down the floor so she can’t walk into a deep seal. Make contact before she gets comfortable on the block. Work around her instead of letting her keep the defender pinned behind her. 
 And the pressure on the passer matters, too. An easy entry pass lets Strack catch where she wants. Active hands and ball pressure can make that passer hesitate and gives the post defender time to improve her position. 
 The goal isn’t to pretend she’ll never get a touch. Make the catch harder and farther from the basket.   
 There’s a difference between defending her after she catches it underneath the rim and making her start a move several feet outside her preferred spot. 
 Then, when she steps out to screen, communicate early. Who has the ball? Who’s staying with Strack? Who’s protecting the rim? 
 Those decisions need to come before the pass does. 
 Another 6-foot-5 problem  
 Ajša Sivka is a 6-foot-5 guard. 
 Yes. A guard. 
 Ajša Sivka is from Slovenia, and she brings size and professional experience from Europe to Kentucky’s perimeter. 
 And yes, Chicago selected her No. 10 in the 2025 WNBA Draft. But let’s clear that up: she never signed with the Sky or played in the WNBA. 
 Now, back to why State needs to account for her. 
 Through Kentucky’s first 2 games, she totaled 23 points and 11 assists. She has the size to see over defenders and the vision to recognize an opening before everybody else realizes it’s there. 
 Her own coach said the quiet part out loud at media day:  
 “She’s going to lead us in turnovers the first half of the year just because everyone else is still trying to get on her page. She sees it a little bit quicker than a lot of players, and sometimes she throws the ball to somebody who’s not looking, but they’re open.” And when Brooks asks her what she saw, she tells him, “They were open.” His answer: “Yeah, but they weren’t looking.” 
 State’s defense should hear that like an invitation. 
 Pressure her handle. Make the passing windows smaller. Stay ready when the ball leaves her hands. 
 See the opportunity. Don’t invent one because you want a steal. 
 A player with that vision can punish a gamble just as quickly as an active defense can disrupt her. 
 Friday’s practice  
 I was at practice Friday morning, and Coach Moore kept coming back to the responsibilities this game will require defensively. 
 Jump to the ball. Be there on the weak side. Rotate on time. Pressure with active hands. 
 Nobody gets to stand in an area and consider the assignment complete. 
 My takeaway? 
 Anticipate. Don’t be late. 
 At one point, Moore stopped the action, stepped in and demonstrated what he wanted. 
 “Come on, baby, throw it to ’em.” 
 That’s the anticipation he’s asking for. Recognize where the pass is headed and be ready to do something about it. 
 Then came the rebounding reminder: 
 “Put your butt on somebody to box out, or put your butt on the bench.” 
 Every former player reading that just sat up a little straighter. 
 I’ve been there. 
 The message is clear… and apparently it was for me, too, because I’m not even playing today and I felt the need to go box somebody out.   
   What Kenny Brooks Just Told Us 
 Kenny Brooks finally talked about State on Thursday night, and he gave away more than he meant to. 
 Kentucky has not shown anything yet. Brooks said he has kept the offense vanilla through two games. No plays run. On purpose, so State does not have extra film to prepare with. 
 His preparation line for State: “Don’t play the score, play the possession.” Minute details. Communication. Get better, don’t relax. 
 That is the other sideline’s version of anticipate, don’t be late. 
 Three things I’m watching 
 Finish the stop. 
 Kentucky’s Savvy Swords collected 16 offensive rebounds across its first 2 games. Add Strack’s presence, and everybody in a State jersey has a rebounding responsibility. 
 The guards have to make contact, too. Watching your post player battle somebody bigger does not help the team.  
 Make the pressure productive. 
 State can disrupt Kentucky’s rhythm, but the possession after the turnover matters just as much. 
 Is the finish available? Is the advance pass there? Or does the offense need to get organized? 
 Run before Kentucky gets comfortable. 
 A set defense with that much size can make the floor feel small. 
 State should look to advance the ball early, fill the lanes and make Kentucky locate everybody while retreating. Even when the first opportunity doesn’t produce a shot, it can create a matchup worth attacking. 
 Now we find out what carries over 
 I like what State has given itself to build on. 
 But today asks more of it: more size to account for, more length in the passing lanes and fewer opportunities to recover from an avoidable mistake. 
 The Pack doesn’t need to become a different team for this matchup. 
 It needs to bring its activity from the opening tip, trust its reads and finish the possessions it works to earn. 
 Two wins got the season started. 
 This one can tell us a little more. 
 3:00PM. ESPN2. 
 Can’t wait.
